name: Practical applications of the lattice framework
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person is working on a technical paper titled "Indexing Without Prediction" (referenced as "indexing-without-prediction-final-2.md") that develops a lattice-theoretic framework for bracketing observable quantities in ordered sequences, with primary applications in atomic spectroscopy and nuclear physics. The paper introduces monotonicity-based deductive brackets, a validity admission test (r = step/σ), a cost ratio V measuring bracket width relative to interpolation error, a superposition detection statistic Σ, and a canonical injective key Λ₁₁ for atomic energy levels. The conversation spanned multiple rounds of increasingly deep technical engagement: first surveying possible applications, then expanding to mathematical and scientific domains, then triaging applications by possibility/plausibility/practicality, then computationally closing a mathematical gap and running candidate paths, and finally reassessing the full application landscape after the gap was closed.

The computational work was substantial. Python scripts were written and executed to verify the closed-form V ≈ 4|y′|/(h|y″|) and its Rydberg specialization V ≈ 4ν/3 + 4/(9ν); to validate this against Ba I 6snf data (parameter-free 0.7% agreement at V = 27.0); to benchmark Σ against Δ⁽³⁾ staggering, Lomb–Scargle, and ACF (finding Σ matches Δ⁽³⁾ at every amplitude and length, eliminating the "superior detector" framing); to test the §4.2 lattice-homomorphism characterisation exhaustively across four lattice types (finding exact agreement between the count of closure-preserving functions depending on both coordinates and the count of cross-coordinate filter containments); to check Sc VI level arithmetic; to evaluate multi-axis bracket intersection on a synthetic nuclear chart (finding median width gain 1.00×, killing that application); and to compute V as a function of sampling stride p at multiple effective quantum numbers. Real quantum defect data for Cs I was sourced from Deiglmayr et al. arXiv:1601.08005.

The final round identified that the closed-form result V = 4|y′|/(h|y″|), now in the draft as Proposition 14.5, has a consequence the draft does not exploit: V is a design variable, not merely a measurement, because h is the experimenter's sampling stride. This reframes the paper's cost analysis entirely. A specific error in §11.2 was identified: the four cells in Ba I's gap (6s13f–16f) share an identical bracket but have V values of 4.90, 33.05, 4.57, and 2.68 respectively — a twelvefold spread — because V depends on the asymmetry of the two steps, not their average. The paper currently treats these four predictions as equivalent, which the closed form directly refutes. Additional findings included: the "18 to 80 times" language surviving at two locations in the draft is stale against the corrected 4.2–57 range now elsewhere in the paper; the Proposition 14.3 claim that the Rydberg floor is unreachable needs the qualifier "consecutive" since non-adjacent neighbours at stride 16 near ν = 21 give V = 2.17; and the §15.4 closing argument has a second leg available — neither ν nor h is expressible in Λ, so both arguments of V lie outside the lattice framework, strengthening the closing thesis at zero cost. Priority ranking settled on: (1) the §11.2 gap-cell recomputation and stride-lever framing, (2) the §4.2 filter-containment characterisation, (3) the Sc VI letter, (4) the nuclear V formula as derivation of the Z-trend. Multi-axis bracketing and Σ-as-superior-detector were confirmed dead.

# Indexing Without Prediction

## Maximality and Empirical Boundary of the Lach Elemental Lattice

---

**Status of this draft.** Prepared for independent review. Every numerical claim
below was computed during the development of this work and is reproducible from
the data sources cited in Appendix C. Section 15 lists claims made in earlier
versions of this framework that are withdrawn. Readers checking this work are
asked to attack **Section 12**, which carries the paper's only open question:
the theorems bound information, the thesis concerns estimation, and the bridge
between them is six empirical failures rather than a proof. A seventh attempt is
the natural attack and §15.4 says what it would have to show.
**Section 10.7**: after §10.6 excludes every superposed channel, the value
ratio *V* rests on four measurements in two domains rather than the nine
channels §10.3 appears to offer. Section 6.4, flagged as the
weakest point in earlier drafts, now carries a theorem rather than a conjecture
and should be checked for the correctness of that proof instead.

---

## Abstract

We construct a lattice Λ₈ over atomic electron configurations, prove it maximal
in a precise sense, and establish empirically that its order structure supplies
no predictive information beyond the coordinates from which it is built.

Λ₈ is a closed distributive lattice of order dimension exactly eight, generated
by an admissibility condition requiring every constraint to take the form
*x ≤ φ(y)* with φ non-decreasing in a single coordinate and a constant floor.
We prove that no further axis can be *derived* from the eight electronic
coordinates: a function whose graph preserves closure is forced to be monotone,
a monotone function's graph is order-isomorphic to the lattice, and the
dimension therefore cannot rise. The lattice is nonetheless
extensible by *independent* physical quantities — the parent ion's total angular
momentum, the total atomic angular momentum, the jK intermediate label, nuclear
spin — each contributing exactly one dimension. Λ₁₁ so constructed is injective
on every test case we have assembled.

Against this we set an empirical result of the opposite sign. A bracketing
method for Rydberg binding energies, derived entirely from *T = Z*²*R*/ν² and
using none of the lattice's order structure, produces containment intervals that
hold in 331 of 331 interior cells across hydrogen, four alkaline earths,
three alkali-like ions, a noble gas and an open-shell transition metal, spanning Z_eff = 1–3, ℓ = 0–5, single-, two-
and multi-limit systems, and both bound and autoionising regimes. Those 331 cells are drawn from approximately 24 channels and are not independent, since cells
within a channel share neighbours. Its uncertainty estimate is derived rather
than calibrated: pooled over the cells carrying one, ±1σ coverage is 68.3%
against a Gaussian expectation of 68.3%, and per-regime coverage runs from 54.5%
to 76.7%. The method's domain boundary reduces to a single ratio — the step
between adjacent measured cells over the measurement error — which we calibrate
and then test off-domain on gas-phase chemical kinetics, where it correctly
predicts the method's failure.

Six independent attempts to extract predictive uplift from the lattice's order —
rank aggregation, comparability, zero-shot subset selection, closure-as-existence,
join-based configuration mixing, and a derived ordinal coordinate — all failed,
each by a distinct and identifiable mechanism. Behind them is a theorem: on a
product order, join, meet and comparability are definable from the coordinates,
so lattice quantities carry no information the coordinates do not. The theorem
bounds information rather than estimation — a deterministic function of the
inputs may still help a finite-sample predictor — so the thesis is the
conjunction of a proved information bound with six empirical failures, and not a
proof of impossibility. It is indifferent to dimension and to how faithfully the
lattice represents the physics. Perfecting the index does not move the predictive
boundary.

The one thing that escapes is deductive containment. A bracket is not a function
of the coordinates of the cell it describes but an entailment from other cells'
coordinates and measured values, and it is the only lattice output we have found
that no coordinate-based control reproduces. Its value is bounded: we prove that
for any monotone sequence the bracket is more than twice as wide as the error of
two-point interpolation between the same neighbours, so an order supplies
containment and never precision. A survey of nine isotopic chains from AME2020
locates the regime where that cost is lowest — neutron-rich nuclei, where pairing
maximises the alternation on which the bound is tight — and shows the ratio
falling systematically with neutron excess while measurement precision holds.

Turning the framework on itself closes it twice. The quantity fixing where the
bracket is cheapest is a ratio of differences of binding energies, and differences
are the one form the lattice's admissibility condition excludes; the same quantity
falls outside the bracketing method's own interiority rule, by 4 to 35 cells in
every chain surveyed. And the sequences in which the bracket appeared cheapest
turn out to be superpositions of two channels — detectable by a diagnostic
requiring no physical input, which flags all nine isotopic chains and the alkane
melting points while returning unity on smooth controls — that the method's own
first rule requires be separated. Separated, the cost ratio returns to 18–80. The
index cannot express, and the method cannot predict, where indexing is useful; and
the one regime where indexing looked useful was a channel that had not been
resolved. That is the sense in which an ordinal structure over configuration space
is useful, and the only sense we have been able to verify.

---

# Part 0 — Origin and Orientation

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Where this began

This framework began as a three-dimensional recoding of the periodic table. Each
element was assigned a triple (*n*, ℓ, *k*): the principal quantum number of the
subshell being filled, its orbital angular momentum, and the occupancy of that
subshell. Under the componentwise partial order, the set of such triples forms a
lattice, and the periodic table becomes a path through it.

The recoding is exact and it is not new physics — it is a bijective relabelling
of information already present in the Madelung filling order. Its interest was
pedagogical and structural: the periodic table's periodicity appears as a
projection of a three-dimensional object, and elements that are chemically
analogous are close in the lattice for a structural reason rather than by
convention.

Three subsequent additions produced the object studied here. Excited
configurations required distinguishing the subshell an electron *leaves* from
the one it *enters*, giving a second triple (*e*, *f*, *g*) — target shell,
target subshell, and number of electrons transferred. Ionisation required a
count *q* of electrons removed from the source. Spin multiplicity required a
coordinate *S*. The result is Λ₈, an eight-dimensional lattice whose cells index
electron configurations relative to a reference state.

The framework's earlier claims concerned prediction: that the lattice's order,
closure and dimension would constrain atomic properties in ways the coordinates
alone did not. This paper reports that those claims are false, establishes why
in a form we believe is a theorem rather than a limitation of effort, and
reports what survives.

### 1.2 What this paper claims

**Structural (Part I).** Λ₈ is closed under join and meet, has order dimension
exactly eight, and is maximal under derivation. It extends by one dimension per
independent physical degree of freedom. As an index of atomic energy levels it
achieves 86% coverage and, at eleven dimensions, injectivity on every test case.
The physical subset of the lattice is *not* a sublattice, and no choice of
coordinates makes it one.

**Empirical (Part II).** A four-rule bracketing method for Rydberg binding
energies, each rule derived from the definition *T = Z*²*R*/ν², produces
deductive containment verified on 331 interior cells across ~24 channels with no
exceptions, and an uncertainty estimate that requires no calibration. Its domain
is bounded by five exclusions, of which three reduce to a single ratio — the step
between adjacent measured cells over the measurement error — yielding an
admission test applicable to any candidate observable before prediction is
attempted. We calibrate that ratio and test it off-domain on gas-phase kinetics,
where the method fails as predicted.

**Thesis (Part III).** The lattice's order structure contributes nothing to the
method. A theorem about product orders shows it can contribute no *information*;
six independent tests found no *estimation* uplift either, each failing by a
mechanism we characterise. The theorem does not depend on the lattice's dimension
or on how faithfully it represents the physics, so improving the index — which we
do in Part I — leaves the predictive boundary exactly where it was.

### 1.3 What this paper does not claim

We do not claim novel physics. Every quantitative result in Part II is a
consequence of the Rydberg formula and the quantum defect; the lattice's role is
to make "interior on some axis" and "same channel" well defined. We do not claim
the method extends to properties other than energies; Section 11 reports two
attempts and both failed, for reasons we characterise. We do not claim the
maximality result in the single-coordinate form asserted in earlier versions;
Section 4.2 gives counterexamples to it and shows why the maximality corollary
does not depend on it.

An earlier line of this work concerned applications to condensed-matter nuclear
phenomena. That material is removed entirely from this paper. It rested on
extensions of Λ₈ whose structural status we now know to be defective
(Appendix A), and revisiting it requires first resolving the multi-target
representation problem.

---

# Part I — Structure

## 2. Construction

### 2.1 The admissibility condition

Let Λ be a subset of ℕ^d defined by a family of constraints. We call the family
**admissible** — the condition previously designated §9.4 — if every constraint
has the form

> *x_i* ≤ φ(*x_j*)  with φ non-decreasing, together with a constant floor
> *x_i* ≥ *c*.

**Proposition 2.1.** *An admissible constraint family defines a set closed under
componentwise join and meet.*

*Proof.* Let *a*, *b* ∈ Λ and consider *x_i* ≤ φ(*x_j*). For the join,
max(*a_i*, *b_i*) = *a_i* or *b_i*; say *a_i*. Then *a_i* ≤ φ(*a_j*) ≤
φ(max(*a_j*, *b_j*)) since φ is non-decreasing. For the meet,
min(*a_i*, *b_i*) ≤ *a_i* ≤ φ(*a_j*), and we require ≤ φ(min(*a_j*, *b_j*)).
Let *w* be whichever of *a*, *b* has the smaller *j*-th coordinate. Then
min(*a_i*, *b_i*) ≤ *w_i* ≤ φ(*w_j*) = φ(min(*a_j*, *b_j*)). A constant floor is preserved by both
operations trivially. ∎

Two consequences shape everything that follows. A bound on a **sum** of two
coordinates is not of admissible form, and generally breaks closure — this is
what defeats the multi-target extension of Appendix A. A **varying floor** is
likewise inadmissible, and this is what places the physical selection rules
outside the language (Section 6.3).

### 2.2 The eight axes

| axis | meaning | bound | form |
|---|---|---|---|
| *n* | source shell | 1 ≤ *n* ≤ *N* | free root |
| ℓ | source subshell | ℓ ≤ *n* − 1 | non-decr. in *n* |
| *k* | source occupancy | 1 ≤ *k* ≤ 2(2ℓ+1) | non-decr. in ℓ |
| *q* | electrons removed | 0 ≤ *q* ≤ *k* | non-decr. in *k* |
| *e* | target shell | 1 ≤ *e* ≤ *E* | free root |
| *f* | target subshell | *f* ≤ *e* − 1 | non-decr. in *e* |
| *g* | electrons transferred | *g* ≤ min(*q*, 2(2*f*+1)) | min of two admissible |
| 2*S* | spin multiplicity | 0 ≤ 2*S* ≤ *k* | non-decr. in *k* |

Derived quantities include the net charge *c* = *q* − *g*, the electron count
*N* = C(*n*,ℓ) + *k* − *c*, and the target occupancy *G*. **These are derived
precisely because they cannot be coordinates**: each is a difference or sum of
two axes, hence not of admissible form. Section 4.3 makes this exact.

### 2.3 Closure and dimension

Closure follows from Proposition 2.1 and was additionally verified on 8 × 10⁶
sampled pairs at caps covering the observed data (*n* ≤ 6, ℓ ≤ 3, *e* ≤ 62,
*f* ≤ 3), with zero failures.

**Order dimension is exactly eight.** The upper bound is immediate: Λ₈ ⊆ ℕ⁸.
The lower bound follows from an explicit 8-box at

> (*n*, ℓ, *k*, *q*, *e*, *f*, *g*, 2*S*) = (3, 1, 2, 1, 2, 0, 0, 0)

all 2⁸ = 256 corners of which are admissible. The box is **cap-independent**: it
remains valid at cap settings (4,2,4,2), (6,3,8,3) and (8,4,12,4).



[[FIG01]]The admissibility (§9.4) constraint graph. Circles are axes; an arrow y → x indicates x is bounded by φ(y). Two roots, n and e, make the graph a forest with a single cross-link at g.




[[FIG02]]The 8-box projected onto four coordinate pairs. Every one of the 256 corners is admissible; labels give the number of corners mapping to each projected point.


### 2.4 A note on cell counts

Earlier versions of this framework reported |Λ₈| = 61,453 as a structural
invariant. It is not. That figure is the cell count at one particular choice of
caps (*n* ≤ 4, ℓ ≤ 2, *e* ≤ 5, *f* ≤ 2), and it changes with them. Every
quantity derived from it — the fraction of cells representing inward
transitions, the fraction "realisable" — is likewise a truncation artefact and
is withdrawn *as a property of Λ₈*. The invariants of Λ₈ are its closure, its
order dimension, and its maximality; its cardinality is not among them.

Such fractions may still be reported as measurements on a **named** enumeration,
and one is (§5.3). The rule observed hereafter is that any figure of the form
"X% of Λ₈" states its caps and claims nothing beyond them. Fractions of this
kind fall monotonically as the cap on *e* rises, because raising that cap adds
only outward cells; no limiting value should be read off them.

## 3. Algebra and geometry, axis by axis

Each axis has an *algebra* — the bound that defines it and its admissible form —
and a *geometry* — the shape of the region it occupies. This section also
reports, for each axis, where it is actually exercised, which turns out to vary
enormously.

**3.1 *n*, the source shell.** Algebra: a free root; every electronic bound
descends from it. Geometry: a chain, 1 to *N*. Exercised: distinguishes species,
but is **constant within any one atom**. In the axis-ablation study (§3.10),
removing *n* from the index of a single species costs zero collisions.

**3.2 ℓ, the source subshell.** Algebra: ℓ ≤ *n* − 1, non-decreasing in *n*.
Geometry: a right triangle in the (*n*, ℓ) plane. Exercised: distinguishes
species and blocks; constant within an atom.

**3.3 *k*, the source occupancy.** Algebra: 1 ≤ *k* ≤ 2(2ℓ+1). Geometry: a
staircase whose width doubles-and-adds-four with ℓ — 2, 6, 10, 14. Exercised:
constant within an atom. *k* is the coordinate that bounds *q*, 2*S*, and (in
Λ₉ and above) the angular momentum axes, so it is structurally central while
being empirically inert within a species.

**3.4 *q*, electrons removed.** Algebra: 0 ≤ *q* ≤ *k*, a triangle nested inside
*k*. Geometry: for each *k*, a chain of length *k*+1. Exercised: separates
neutral from ionised species. Constant (*q* = 1) across all singly-excited
states of one atom.

**3.5 *e*, the target shell.** Algebra: a second free root. Geometry: a chain.
Exercised: **this is the workhorse.** Removing *e* from the Ca I index costs 13
collisions in 27 levels; from Kr I, 22 in 46. It is the axis the bracketing
method of Part II interpolates along, and the only axis that is load-bearing
both across and within species.

**3.6 *f*, the target subshell.** Algebra: *f* ≤ *e* − 1, a second right
triangle independent of the (*n*, ℓ) one. Geometry: the Λ₈ region is therefore a
product of two triangles, not a single simplex — this is the clearest sense in
which the lattice is not merely a relabelled periodic table. Exercised: 7
collisions on removal for Ca I, 22 for Kr I. Load-bearing.

**3.7 *g*, electrons transferred.** Algebra: *g* ≤ min(*q*, 2(2*f*+1)) — the
intersection of two triangles, a wedge. Geometry: the only axis bounded by two
others simultaneously. Exercised: **zero collisions on removal.** For
singly-excited states *g* = *q* = 1 universally, so the axis is exercised only by
doubly-excited configurations, of which the observational record contains few.

**3.8 2*S*, spin.** Algebra: 0 ≤ 2*S* ≤ *k*. Geometry: a chain over *k*.
Exercised: 5 collisions on removal for Ca I. Load-bearing where LS coupling
holds; **undefined** for jK-coupled systems such as Kr I, where the paper must
substitute the parent's *J*.

**3.9 The collective whole.** Λ₈ is a product of two triangular regions —
(*n*, ℓ) and (*e*, *f*) — with occupancy chains hung from each, and a wedge
(*g*) linking them. It is *not* a simplex, *not* a hypercube, and *not* a chain
product; the two roots make it a forest-shaped constraint graph with a single
cross-link. The simplest complete picture is Figure 3.



[[FIG03]]Λ₈ decomposed: two triangular blocks, two chains descending from k, and one cross-link where g is bounded by both q and f.



### 3.10 Axis ablation

 Removing each axis in turn from the index and counting
collisions gives a direct measurement of what each contributes.

| axis | Ca I (27 levels) | Kr I (46 levels) |
|---|---|---|
| *n*, ℓ, *k*, *q*, *g* | 0 collisions | 0 collisions |
| *e* | **13** | **22** |
| *f* | **7** | **22** |
| 2*S* | **5** | undefined |
| 2*J*_c | 0 (fixed) | **20** |
| 2*J* | **12** | **35** |

Six of ten coordinates are constant within a species and discriminate only
*across* species. Only *e* and *f* appear in both roles — which is precisely why
the method of Part II interpolates in *e* at fixed *f* and uses no other axis.

**What a path through the lattice looks like.** A chain in Λ₈ is a sequence of
cells each below the next, so every coordinate is non-decreasing along it and
exactly one advances at each step. Such a path is readable as physics. The one
in Figure 16 runs from H 1s to Ca I 4s5d ³D in fourteen steps: *n* climbs from 1
to 4, taking the source shell through the ground configurations of H, Li, Na and
K; *k* rises to 2, closing the 4s shell at Ca; *q* rises to 1, promoting one
electron; *e* and *f* climb to 5 and 2, carrying it to the 5d target; *g* places
it; and 2*S* rises to 2, coupling the pair as a triplet. Every intermediate cell
satisfies §9.4 admissibility, and the first five are ground configurations of
real elements rather than formal way-points.

[[FIG16]]A monotone path through Λ₈, from H 1s to Ca I 4s5d ³D. Each column is one cell of the chain; each row is one of the eight coordinates. A filled cell marks the coordinate that advances at that step, and the bar beneath each row spans the steps over which that axis is active. The strip below labels the cells that correspond to real configurations. The inset confirms what the order requires: no coordinate ever decreases.

**A second division cuts across the first, and Part II depends on it silently.**
An axis can supply a *bracket* only if it takes three or more values in the
data, since a bracket needs a measured neighbour on each side. That splits the
ten coordinates three ways:

| kind | axes | can index? | can bracket? |
|---|---|---|---|
| interpolation | *e*, *f* | yes | yes |
| indexing only | 2*S*, 2*J*_c, 2*J* | yes | no |
| inert within a species | *n*, ℓ, *k*, *q*, *g* | no | no |

The middle row is structural rather than a limitation of the data. Core *J*
takes exactly two values for a p⁵ core, so **every cell is an endpoint on that
axis**, and no quantity of further measurement would change it. The Kr I
(²P°₁⁄₂) 6p cell illustrates the whole table: it has two neighbours on *e* — 5p
and 7p, both measured — one on *f*, since 6s is present and 6d is not, and a
measured partner on 2*J*_c that can never help. Rule 1's "interior on some axis"
is therefore satisfiable only on the first row, and the ablation study above
measured the split without naming it.

[[FIG04]]Axis ablation for an LS-coupled species (Ca I) and a jK-coupled one (Kr I). Six of ten coordinates are inert within a species.


## 4. Maximality under derivation

### 4.1 The two lemmas

The result is stated as two facts because they carry very unequal weight, and
the combined form disguises which is which. Neither requires *L* to be a product
of chains, and neither requires interval-closure.

**Lemma 4.1 (the substantive half).** *Let L be a finite lattice and h : L → ℤ a
function whose graph G = {(x, h(x))} is closed under componentwise join and
meet. Then h is monotone.*

*Proof.* Closure puts (*x* ∨ *y*, max(*h*(*x*), *h*(*y*))) in *G*. Since *G* is
the graph of a function its second component is determined by its first, so
*h*(*x* ∨ *y*) = max(*h*(*x*), *h*(*y*)). If *x* ≤ *y* then *x* ∨ *y* = *y*,
giving *h*(*y*) = max(*h*(*x*), *h*(*y*)) ≥ *h*(*x*). ∎

**Lemma 4.2 (bookkeeping).** *If h : L → ℤ is monotone then x ↦ (x, h(x)) is an
order isomorphism onto G, and dim(G) = dim(L).*

*Proof.* The map is a bijection onto *G*, order-preserving by monotonicity, and
order-reflecting because the projection forgetting the last coordinate is
monotone. Order dimension is an isomorphism invariant. ∎

**Corollary 4.3.** *No ninth axis derived from the eight electronic coordinates
can be adjoined to Λ₈ while preserving closure and raising the dimension.* A
derived axis is a function of the cell, so its graph is order-isomorphic to Λ₈
and the dimension is unchanged — always. An *independent* quantity assigns
several values to one cell, so the adjoined set is not a function graph; it can
raise the dimension, and does so exactly when its bound is admissible (§5).

**Exhaustive verification.** On a nine-element sublattice of a product of two
chains that is deliberately *not* interval-closed — {(*n*, ℓ) : 1 ≤ *n* ≤ 4,
0 ≤ ℓ ≤ min(*n*−1, 2)}, for which (1,1) lies componentwise between (1,0) and
(2,1) yet violates ℓ ≤ *n* − 1 — every function into a three-valued codomain was
enumerated. Of 19,683 functions, 19,573 are non-monotone and **none** of those
has a closed graph, confirming Lemma 4.1. Of 546 monotone functions into a
four-valued codomain, **all 546** induce an order isomorphism onto their graph
with zero order mismatches, confirming Lemma 4.2. Exact order dimension computed
from minimum realizers gives dim(*L*) = 2, and dim(*G*) = 2 for every one of the
25 closure-preserving functions at three values and every one of the 65 at four
values. **Zero** raise the dimension.

### 4.2 What the earlier statement got wrong

Earlier versions of this framework asserted a stronger result: that a
closure-preserving *h* must be a monotone function of a **single** coordinate.
That claim is true for products of chains, where the sublevel sets are principal
down-sets and consecutive generators can be shown to differ in one coordinate.
**It is false for sublattices of products of chains, and Λ₈ is a sublattice.**

On the nine-element test lattice above, 3 of the 25 closure-preserving functions
at three values depend on both coordinates, as do 14 of the 65 at four values.
An explicit counterexample:

> *h*(1,0) = *h*(2,0) = *h*(2,1) = 0;  *h*(3,0) = *h*(3,1) = *h*(4,0) =
> *h*(4,1) = 1;  *h*(3,2) = *h*(4,2) = 2.

Its graph is closed under both operations. It depends on *n*, since
*h*(2,1) ≠ *h*(3,1); and on ℓ, since *h*(3,1) ≠ *h*(3,2). The old proof fails at
the step *m_v* + *e_i* ∈ *L*, which requires incrementing one coordinate to stay
inside *L* — exactly what interval-closure would supply and what a sublattice
does not.

**The corollary survives the loss of the theorem.** Redundancy of derived axes
never needed the single-coordinate property; it needed only that the dimension
not rise, and Lemma 4.2 delivers that from monotonicity alone. The
counterexamples are closure-preserving functions of several coordinates that are
*still* dimension-redundant. The earlier proof was establishing a stronger
statement than the argument required, and paying for it with a hypothesis Λ₈
does not satisfy.

### 4.3 Rejected candidates

Each of the following was proposed as a ninth axis in earlier work and each
fails, with the failure now attributable to Lemma 4.1 rather than to
case-by-case testing.

| candidate | form | join fail | meet fail | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *h* = *n* | projection | 0 | 0 | closed but redundant, no 9-box |
| *h* = 2*n* | monotone in *n* | 0 | 0 | closed but redundant |
| *h* = *n* + ℓ | two coordinates | 42,492 | 42,492 | breaks closure |
| *h* = *q* − *g* (net charge *c*) | difference | 284,858 | 284,858 | breaks closure |
| *h* = *k* − *q* | difference | 406,400 | 406,400 | breaks closure |
| *h* = *e* − *f* | difference | 266,440 | 266,440 | breaks closure |
| *h* = ⌊*C*/*e*²⌋ (energy proxy) | anti-monotone | 503,404 | 503,404 | breaks closure |

The energy proxy deserves separate comment because it was the original
motivation for a ninth "output" axis. It fails for a reason sharper than
inadmissibility: energy *decreases* with *e* while the order *increases*, so an
energy-valued coordinate is anti-monotone and pairs of cells acquire no upper
bound at all. **A metric quantity that increased with the coordinates might well
be admissible.** The obstruction is the sign, not the metricity — a correction
to the analysis of metric coordinates in earlier versions of this framework.

## 5. Extension by independent quantities

### 5.1 Three classes

Lemmas 4.1–4.2 constrain only *functions of the existing coordinates*. Quantities
that are physically independent escape it. Candidates fall into three classes:

- **(a) Functions of existing coordinates.** Either inadmissible, or
  closure-preserving and hence monotone — in which case the graph is
  order-isomorphic to Λ₈ and the axis is dimensionally redundant, whether or not
  it depends on one coordinate. Corollary 4.3.
- **(b) Independent, bounded by an existing coordinate.** Admissible if and only
  if the bound has §9.4 form. Contributes exactly one dimension.
- **(c) Independent, bounded by a constant.** The admissible set is a direct
  product; closure is automatic; contributes one dimension.

### 5.2 Λ₉, Λ₁₀, Λ₁₁

**Parent-ion angular momentum (class b).** The same electronic cell can leave
the residual ion in different *J* states, so *J*_c is not a function of the
eight. With the bound 2*J*_c ≤ *k* — non-decreasing in a single coordinate — the
enlarged set is **closed exactly**: 6,989 cells, all 24,419,566 pairs tested,
zero failures. A 9-box exists at (3,1,5,4,3,1,3,2,1). **Order dimension 9.**

**Total atomic angular momentum (class b).** With 2*J* ≤ 2*k*, closure holds on
2,041,470 cells with zero failures and a 10-box at (3,1,2,1,2,0,0,0,0,0).
**Order dimension 10.**

**jK intermediate label (class b).** Required for jK-coupled systems; bounded
loosely by 2*K* ≤ 2*k*.

**Nuclear spin (class c).** Bounded by a constant; the set is a direct product;
closure automatic.

### 5.3 What extension buys and costs

| lattice | Kr I core-*J* collisions | Ca I fine-structure collisions |
|---|---|---|
| Λ₈ | 3 (of 3 cells) | 1 |
| Λ₉ | **0** | 1 |
| Λ₁₀ | 0 | **0** |
| Λ₁₁ | 0 | 0 |

On a 46-level Kr I test set: Λ₈ gives 7 cells with 39 collisions; Λ₉, 11 cells
with 35; Λ₁₀, 34 cells with 12; **Λ₁₁, 46 cells with 0**.

The cost is looseness. Each class-(b) bound admits more than the physics
requires: the true range for total *J* is the triangle rule
|*J*_c − *j*| ≤ *J* ≤ *J*_c + *j*, whose **lower bound varies with the cell**,
and §9.4 permits only constant floors. Measured on the enumeration *n* ≤ 4,
ℓ ≤ 2, *e* ≤ 5, *f* ≤ 2, the physically realisable fraction is 23.3% at eight
dimensions, 9.0% at nine, 1.7% at ten.

Those three levels are cap-dependent in the sense of §2.4 and are not properties
of Λ₈. What is offered here is the *ratio* between them — each added dimension
costs roughly a factor of three in realisable fraction — and even that is
measured at one choice of caps and has not been tested for cap-invariance. It is
reported as the price of the collisions cleared in the table above, not as a
structural constant.

## 6. The lattice as an index

### 6.1 Coverage

For each species we map observed configurations to Λ cells and count how many
map at all.

| species | mapped | coverage |

| Kr I | 9/9 | 100% |
| Sc III | 8/8 | 100% |
| Ba II | 10/10 | 100% |
| Sr I | 9/10 | 90% |
| Ca I | 12/15 | 80% |
| Ti I | 6/11 | 55% |
| **total** | **54/63** | **86%** |

Every failure is a **multi-subshell configuration** — two occupied non-source
subshells, which a single (*e*, *f*, *g*) triple cannot name. Coverage is a
representational limit and **no additional coordinate repairs it**; the natural
repair, a second target triple, breaks the lattice (Appendix A).

### 6.2 Injectivity

Three collision types, each cleared by a specific axis:

| type | example | resolved by | at |
|---|---|---|---|
| core *J* | Kr I (²P°₃⁄₂)5s vs (²P°₁⁄₂)5s | 2*J*_c | Λ₉ |
| fine structure | Ca I 4s4d ³D₁,₂,₃ | 2*J* | Λ₁₀ |
| jK label | Kr I 5p ²[1/2] vs ²[3/2], same *J* | *K* | Λ₁₁ |

The first is consequential beyond bookkeeping. The two Kr I channels converge on
limits **5,370 cm⁻¹ apart**, and the method of Part II requires knowing which.
**Λ₈ cannot supply that assignment**; in the work reported here it was read from
the ASD configuration string. Λ₉ supplies it.

### 6.3 The physical set is not a sublattice

The physically realisable cells of Λ₈ are those satisfying the spin selection
rules: 2*S* ≡ *k* (mod 2), and 2*S* ≤ min(*k*, 2(2ℓ+1) − *k*).

**This set is not closed.** In the (*k*, 2*S*) plane, (1,1) and (2,0) are both
physical; their join (2,1) is not, because 2*S* must be even when *k* is even.
Failures: 1 at ℓ = 0, 15 at ℓ = 1, 70 at ℓ = 2.

The obstruction is structural. A **congruence** is not an inequality, and §9.4
admits only inequalities with constant floors. The selection rules of atomic
physics — spin parity, hole symmetry, the triangle rule — are none of them of
that form.

### 6.4 Offset coordinates: faithful but not closed

*This section reports a negative result obtained late in the work and it
corrects an intermediate claim.*

One may attempt to bring the selection rules inside the language by
reparameterisation. Replace 2*S* by the paired-unit count *m* = (*k* − 2*S*)/2,
so that 2*S* = *k* − 2*m* carries the parity of *k* automatically; replace 2*J*
by the triangle offset *t* = (2*J* − |2*J*_c − 2*j*|)/2, so that the triangle
rule is satisfied by construction. Each transformation is bijective, so the
dimension is unchanged and Lemma 4.2 is untouched.

Tested **in isolation**, each appears to work: the (*k*, *m*) plane is closed at
every fixed ℓ, and the (*J*_c, *j*, *t*) block is closed with 140 cells and zero
failures.

**Assembled into one lattice, they do not.** Exhaustive test on 1,431 cells and
all 1,023,165 pairs: **222,075 join failures and 11,696 meet failures.** The two
failure modes have different causes, and they separate cleanly.

*The join failures come from a ceiling that decreases.* The bound
2*J*_c ≤ *k* − *q* falls as *q* rises. Taking the join raises *q*, lowering the
ceiling, while simultaneously raising 2*J*_c — so the join escapes. The meet
lowers both and is safe. On the (*k*, *q*, *J*_c) block alone: 2,640 join
failures, **zero** meet failures.

*The meet failures come from a floor that decreases in ℓ.* Rewriting §6.3's
selection rules in the offset coordinate gives *m* ≥ max(0, *k* − (2ℓ+1)).
Taking the meet lowers ℓ, which *raises* the floor, while simultaneously
lowering *m* — so the meet escapes. The join is safe. On the (ℓ, *k*, *m*) block
alone: **zero** join failures, 98 meet failures at ℓ ≤ 3, every one of them a
violation of this floor.

**A correction to how this was previously stated.** The obstruction is not that
the floor varies with *k*. A floor varying with *k* alone is harmless: freezing
the ℓ-term at its maximum gives *m* ≥ max(0, *k* − 7), and that lattice is
closed under both operations with zero failures of either kind. What breaks meet
is the dependence on ℓ, and it breaks meet precisely because it runs *against*
the order — the floor rises exactly where the meet is taking the coordinate
down. Both bounds violate §9.4, which admits decreasing behaviour in neither
place: ceilings must be non-decreasing, and floors must be constant.

This also explains why the isolation tests passed. Holding ℓ fixed while
checking the (*k*, *m*) plane holds fixed the one coordinate whose variation
carries the obstruction. The lesson is narrower and more useful than "isolated
closure does not imply joint closure": an isolation test must vary every
coordinate appearing in the bound under test, including those that appear only
as parameters.

What the offset coordinates do achieve is worth recording. All 1,431 cells decode
to genuine physical states — zero violations — and the encoding is injective,
1,903 distinct states with no duplicates. **Offset coordinates are a faithful and
injective parameterisation of the physical set that is not a lattice.**

It is tempting to state the section's result as *one may have closure or
faithfulness, not both.* Unqualified that is false, and the counterexample is
trivial: any finite set of physical states can be enumerated along a chain,
which is a lattice and a bijective parameterisation at once. Earlier versions of
this section dismissed that counterexample by asserting that a chain enumeration
is not admissible. That assertion is wrong — a chain has image {0,…,N−1}, cut
out by a constant floor and a constant ceiling, which is admissible form under
§2.1 exactly as written.

The counterexample fails for a different reason, and identifying it converts the
claim from a conjecture into a theorem. A chain enumeration is *bijective* but
destroys the order; what §6.3 and §6.4 are really about is whether an admissible
coordinate system can reproduce the physical set **as an ordered object**.

> **Theorem 6.1.** *No admissible coordinate system is order-isomorphic to the
> physical set.*
>
> *Proof.* An admissible family is closed under componentwise join and meet
> (Proposition 2.1). In ℕ^d the componentwise join of two elements is their least
> upper bound, so a set containing it possesses that join in the induced order:
> an admissible set is a lattice. Order isomorphism is defined purely
> order-theoretically and therefore preserves joins and meets. The physical set
> is not a lattice — at ℓ = 1 the pair (1,1), (2,0) has two incomparable minimal
> upper bounds, (2,2) and (3,1), so no least upper bound exists. Hence no
> admissible set is order-isomorphic to it. ∎

The third step needs care, because §6.3 shows only that the physical set is not
closed under *componentwise* join, which is weaker than not being a lattice: a
least upper bound might exist as some other element. Checked directly, it does
not. Pairs with no least upper bound number 1 at ℓ = 0, 15 at ℓ = 1 and 70 at
ℓ = 2; the ℓ = 0 case has no upper bound at all, and from ℓ = 1 upward the
failure is the two-minimal-upper-bounds pattern above.

This also explains why the offset coordinates of this section are not a
counterexample either, using a fact already established: *m* = (*k* − 2*S*)/2 is
order-**reversing** in *S*, verified at 140 of 140 pairs. Offset coordinates are
bijective but not order-isomorphic, and they sit precisely in the gap between the
two readings of "faithful" that Theorem 6.1 now separates.

What can be stated without qualification is weaker and still worth having.
**Offset coordinates are a faithful and injective parameterisation of the
physical set that is not a lattice**, and the lattice of §2 properly contains a
physical set that is not a sublattice of it. The two objects are genuinely
different, and §6.3 and §6.4 together show that the difference is not an
artefact of how the coordinates were written down.

# Part II — A Bracketing Method for Rydberg Energies

## 7. Derivation

Every rule below follows from one expression:

> *T* = *Z*_eff² *R* / ν²,  ν = *n* − δ(*n*, ℓ, core)

where *T* is the binding energy of the outer electron relative to its series
limit and δ the quantum defect. The method uses the lattice only to make two
notions well defined: which cells belong to the same **channel** (fixed source,
fixed parent state, fixed *f*), and which cells are **interior** on an axis.

## 8. The four rules

> **Rule 1 — Interiority.** Predict only cells belonging to the same Rydberg
> sequence as their neighbours, and either interior on some axis — a measured
> neighbour on each side — or **above** the highest measured member. Extrapolation
> **below** the lowest measured member is forbidden.
>
> **Rule 2 — Variable.** Read the interpolation variable off *T* = *Z*²*R*/ν²
> for the axis in question: *E* along *n* within a series; interval ratios along
> *J*; geometric in *T* along the core shell.
>
> **Rule 3 — Separation.** Report the deductive bracket separately from the
> inferential point estimate. Given monotonicity, the true value cannot lie
> outside [max below, min above].
>
> **Rule 4 — Uncertainty.** Fit δ locally by a Ritz expansion and take
> σ = 2*R Z*_eff² · SE_pred / ν³ from the fit's prediction standard error. Fit
> the highest-order term the neighbour count supports: δ = δ₀ + δ₂/*n*² where
> three or more neighbours exist, δ = δ₀ where only two do.

**Rule 4's clause on fit order matters at the edge of a channel.** The
two-parameter Ritz form needs three neighbours to leave a residual, and a
channel with exactly three members has an interior cell with only two. The Kr I
(²P°₁⁄₂) *n*p series is the one such case in this paper: 5p, 6p and 7p, with 6p
interior. Under the constant-defect form the cell returns an estimate in error
by −70.9 cm⁻¹ against σ = 602 cm⁻¹, or 0.12σ. It is a valid cell and an almost
worthless one — its bracket spans 14,602 cm⁻¹ because its neighbours are two
principal quantum numbers away — and it is the clearest instance in Part II's
own data of the validity/value distinction developed in §10.3.

**Rule 1's second clause is not redundant.** Sc III 3d is interior in *n* within
ℓ = 2, yet including it inflates the median error by 3.2× because it is the
collapsed ground state rather than a sequence member. The operational test is
that its defect departs from its neighbours' by 0.14 where they depart from each
other by 0.008 — a factor of 17.

**Justification of each rule by ablation:**

| rule violated | cost |
|---|---|
| extrapolate **below** the series | median error 0.46 → 206 cm⁻¹ (**446×**), *n* = 6 |
| extrapolate **above** the series | median error 0.46 → 0.13 cm⁻¹ (**0.28×**), *n* = 6 |
| wrong interpolation variable | rms 200 → 588 cm⁻¹ (2.9×) |
| pooled σ instead of per-cell | ±1σ coverage 96.2% instead of 69.6% |
| include collapsed orbital | median error 12.8 → 41.3 cm⁻¹ (3.2×) |

**The extrapolation cost is directional, and a single figure conceals it.** An
earlier version quoted 3.7× on pooled rms over all twelve extrapolated cells.
That statistic is not reproducible and is unstable: on the same data it is 18.8×
on rms, 4.6× on median, and **0.5× if the two worst cells are removed** — an rms
over twelve points containing a 12,942 cm⁻¹ outlier is not a summary that should
carry a rule. Split by direction the instability disappears. Extrapolating below
a series costs 446× on median, because δ varies fastest at low *n* and the Ritz
fit run backwards diverges; extrapolating above costs 0.28×, because δ has
already flattened. The asymmetry is a factor of 1,577 and Rule 1 is stated
accordingly.

This also clarifies the Ba I 6s8f prediction of §11.2, which is an interior cell
in a gap rather than an extrapolation.

## 9. Verification

**331 interior cells, bracket exact in every one** — 295 in the species below, and a further 36 in the open-shell test of §9.1.

Two counts are reported and they differ, because a bracket and a σ have
different data requirements. A bracket needs one measured neighbour on each
side: **295 cells** have one. The local Ritz fit δ = δ₀ + δ₂/*n*² has two free
parameters and needs three neighbours to leave a residual; where only two exist
the fit drops to a constant defect, which has one parameter and one degree of
freedom. Under that rule **all 295 cells also carry a σ**. Coverage percentages
below are over cells carrying a σ from the two-parameter form.

| regime | cells | bracket | ±1σ | median error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| H I (*Z*_eff = 1) | 5 | 5/5 | — | **0.006 cm⁻¹** † |
| Mg/Ca/Sr/Ba I, Ca/Sr/Ba II | 226 | 226/226 | 68.1% | 1.05 |
| Ca I 3d channel (autoionising) | 22 | 22/22 | 68.2% | 9.37 |
| Kr I (multi-limit p-block) | 31 | 31/31 | 76.7% | 3.54 |
| Sc III (*Z*_eff = 3) | 11 | 11/11 | 54.5% | 12.8 |

† The hydrogen row uses the reduced-mass Rydberg *R*_H = 109 678.7717 cm⁻¹,
which for hydrogen *is* the ionisation limit, so the quantum defect vanishes
identically — measured defects span −2 × 10⁻⁵ to 0. Substituting the
infinite-mass *R*_∞ = 109 737.3 cm⁻¹ breaks that identity by the 58.5 cm⁻¹
reduced-mass difference, manufactures a spurious defect of ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁴ and
inflates the median error 54-fold to 0.34 cm⁻¹. For the heavier species the
correction is 10⁻⁵ relative and is absorbed into the fitted defect, so the choice
is invisible; hydrogen is the one row where it is not. The 0.006 cm⁻¹ figure is
therefore a measurement of the *data*, not of the method, and sets the floor
below which no result in Part II can be interpreted.

Spanning *Z*_eff = 1, 2, 3; ℓ = 0 through 5; single-, two- and multi-limit
systems; bound and autoionising states.

**On independence.** These 331 cells are drawn from approximately **24
channels** — 22 in the species above and two in the open-shell test of §9.1.
Cells within a channel share neighbours, so successive brackets are correlated
and 331 should not be read as 331 independent tests. The honest figure is 331
cells across 24 channels.

**The two datasets are correlated differently, and the Sc I addition sharpens
rather than dilutes the count.** The original 22 channels average 13 cells each,
with the largest contributing 22. The Sc I ²P° channel alone contributes 28, so
it is the single largest block in the paper and its 28 brackets are the most
strongly correlated set here. A reader who discounts within-channel correlation
entirely — counting one effective test per channel — gets 24 rather than 331,
and the bracket holds in all 24. That is the most conservative reading available
and it is the one we would defend.

**On the bracket's robustness.** Perturbing the series limit by ±5 cm⁻¹ leaves
bracket coverage unchanged at 15/15 in a test case, because the bracket uses only
measured neighbours. The point estimate and σ require the limit; **the bracket
does not**. Similarly, "interior" requires that neighbours exist, not that they
be adjacent: with *n* = 8–16 removed from a Ba I series, cell 17 still brackets
correctly, at width 2,012 cm⁻¹ instead of 400.

**On the neighbour count.** The Ritz fit uses the *k* nearest members. Sensitivity:
rms 14.0 / 17.1 / 15.8 / 15.5 / 15.5 cm⁻¹ for *k* = 3, 4, 6, 8, 10. No strong
preference; *k* = 6 was chosen arbitrarily and the paper reports the sensitivity
rather than presenting it as derived.

### 9.1 An open-shell test: Sc I

Ti I fails for want of interior cells (§10 iii), and earlier versions of this
paper left open whether that was a property of Ti I or of the open-shell block.
**Sc I settles it.** Its ground configuration 3d4s² has a single d electron and
therefore far fewer parent terms than Ti I's 3d², and its Rydberg series converge
on Sc II 3d4s ¹D₂ at 55,463.0 cm⁻¹ and ³D₁ at 52,922.0 cm⁻¹.

The 3d4s(¹D)*n*p ²P° channel runs from **n = 9 to n = 38 — thirty members on a
single resolved parent**, the longest channel in this paper. The ²D° channel of
the same parent adds ten more. Applying the four rules without modification:

| channel | members | interior | bracket | median error | ±1σ | ±2σ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3d4s(¹D)*n*p ²P°, *n* = 9–38 | 30 | 28 | **28 / 28** | 0.163 cm⁻¹ | 64.3% | 96.4% |
| 3d4s(¹D)*n*p ²D°, *n* = 9–18 | 10 | 8 | **8 / 8** | 1.541 | 50.0% | 87.5% |

with minimum *r* = 11 against an admission threshold of 5. **The domain statement
therefore extends to open-shell systems**, and Ti I's failure is a property of
Ti I — seven parent terms, series terminating at *n* = 5 or 6, levels 40–50%
configuration-mixed — rather than of the open shell.

**A second observation, which the channel makes unusually visible.** The quantum
defect of the ²P° series looks ragged: it drifts by 0.19 across the thirty
members, with single steps reaching 0.11. That is not structure. Because
dδ/d*T* = ν³/2*R*, the quoted level uncertainty of 0.6 cm⁻¹ at *n* = 38 maps to
0.127 in the defect, and 26 of 29 steps lie within three times their propagated
uncertainty. **The estimator feels the ν³ amplification and the bracket does
not**, because the bracket uses measured neighbours directly and never
differentiates. That is the asymmetry of §14, appearing in a system this work had
not previously tested: the bracket holds at 28/28 on a sequence whose defect
sequence looks disordered.

## 10. Domain and exclusions

**Verified domain.** Binding energies of Rydberg series: one electron outside a
core in a definite state, channel by channel, with the channel's limit supplied
by the configuration label. Interior cells only, excluding collapsed orbitals.

**Five exclusions. They are not five mechanisms.** One breaks monotonicity; three
are the same resolution failure at different values of one ratio; one is a
data-hygiene condition. §10.1 makes the reduction precise.

**(i) Sign-changing quantities.** Any property built from a matrix element that
passes through zero cannot be monotone. Sr I 5s²¹S₀ → 5s*n*p ¹P₁ reduced
transition probabilities collapse by a **factor of 60** at *n* = 6 and recover —
a Cooper-type node. Bracket coverage across the node: 79%. Away from it: 100%
on 11 cells. This is the only exclusion that attacks the order hypothesis
itself.

**(ii) Quantities monotone in neither direction.** Fine-structure splittings
reduced by ν³ drift by 3 to 22% across a series while reversing direction
locally: Ca II *n*d increases at 2 of 7 steps, Ba II *n*d at 2 of 6, Ba II *n*p
at 3 of 6. Bracket coverage over the 17 interior cells is **58.8%** under the
direction-agnostic bracket that Rule 3 specifies.

An earlier version reported 35.3% and attributed the failure to flatness; both
are corrected here. The 35.3% is not reproducible under any bracket convention
we have tried — a directional bracket applied to these mostly-decreasing
sequences gives 41.2% and Rule 3's min/max form gives 58.8% — and the earlier
discussion of a figure lying *below* the 50% floor of §10.1 is therefore moot.
The mechanism is not flatness. That floor applies to a flat sequence with
independent noise, and these sequences are not flat; **they are monotone in
neither direction**, and a sequence monotone in neither direction cannot be
bracketed at all. That is a simpler and stronger exclusion than the one it
replaces, and it removes this case from the one-ratio reduction of §10.1, which
now covers three exclusions rather than four.

**(iii) Systems without interior cells.** Ti I: 23 channels, 26 members, **zero
interior cells**. This is a statement about Ti I and not about open-shell systems
in general — §9.1 applies the method to a thirty-member channel in Sc I without
modification. No channel reaches three members, because the ionisation limit
near 55,000 cm⁻¹ sits below the onset of severe level density, and above
~42,000 cm⁻¹ the levels are 40–50% configuration-mixed and have no assignable
parent. The method declines rather than errs. This is the degenerate case of
(ii): where no interior cell exists, no step exists to resolve.

**(iv) Collapsed orbitals.** Excluded by the defect-departure test of Rule 1. A
data-hygiene condition, not a property of the observable.

**(v) Insufficient measurement precision.** An observable may be monotone, free
of zeros, and vary by orders of magnitude, and the bracket still fails — because
containment is a claim about *true* neighbours and one only ever has *measured*
ones. Tested off-domain on gas-phase kinetics (§10.2): the deductive guarantee
degrades continuously, and does so as a function of a single ratio.

### 10.1 The five reduce to one ratio

Let *r* = (fractional step between adjacent measured cells) / (fractional 1σ
measurement error). Exclusion (ii) shrinks the numerator; (v) inflates the
denominator; (iii) is *r* undefined. Only *r* appears. Simulating three
consecutive monotone true values spaced *r*σ apart, with independent Gaussian
error on the two neighbours, gives a one-parameter containment curve:

| *r* = step/σ | 0.1 | 0.5 | 1.0 | 1.3 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 4.0 | ≥5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| containment | 50.3% | 57.3% | 73.3% | 82.5% | 95.6% | 99.7% | 100.0% | 100.0% |

The curve has a closed form and needs no simulation. With independent Gaussian
error on the two neighbours and none on the target,

> P(contained) = Φ(*r*)² + (1 − Φ(*r*))²,

the first term being the case where both measured neighbours fall on their
correct sides and the second where both fall on the wrong side and straddle the
target in reverse.

**Real channels have unequal steps, and the form generalises.** Writing *r*₋ and
*r*₊ for the two fractional steps either side of the target, each over the
fractional 1σ error,

> P(contained) = Φ(*r*₋)·Φ(*r*₊) + (1 − Φ(*r*₋))·(1 − Φ(*r*₊)),

which reduces to the expression above when *r*₋ = *r*₊. The single-*r* form,
evaluated at min(*r*₋, *r*₊), is a **lower bound**: it discards the information
that the larger step is better resolved. The two forms coincide for the Rydberg
series of Part II, where consecutive steps differ by a few per cent, and diverge
by up to nine points for the kinetics channel of §10.2, where they differ by a
factor of two. The admission threshold is stated on min(*r*₋, *r*₊) throughout,
which is the conservative choice. An earlier draft simulated this and mis-transcribed the
*r* = 1.3 entry as 84%; the exact value is 82.51%, and every other entry
reproduces to three decimals. Exact values at the threshold are 99.7304% at
*r* = 3, 99.9937% at 4 and 99.999943% at 5.

The admission threshold of *r* ≥ 5 used throughout is read from this curve:
containment is 99.7% at *r* = 3 and indistinguishable from 100% at *r* ≥ 4 in
4 × 10⁵ draws, so 5 is the smallest integer that leaves a margin. Nothing in the
paper's conclusions turns on the choice between 4 and 5; the channels tested
either clear it by an order of magnitude or fail it outright.

The floor at *r* → 0 is exactly 1/2, and it is a theorem rather than a simulated
value: at *r* = 0 the two measured neighbours are independent draws about a
common mean, and the target lies between them precisely when they straddle it,
with probability 2 · (1/2)(1/2) = 1/2. **This curve is the domain boundary of Part II**, and it is why
*T* = *Z*²*R*/ν² works.

The margin is large but not uniform, and an earlier version of this section
overstated it. Low-lying levels from Fourier-transform work are good to
~10⁻³ cm⁻¹, giving *r* of order 10⁵–10⁶. The high-*n* Rydberg members that the
method actually interpolates are not: for the Ba I 6s*n*f ³F₂ series, Curry's
compilation draws *n* ≥ 9 from Armstrong *et al.*, whose stated typical
uncertainty is of order 0.1 cm⁻¹, and the published values are quoted to between
one and three decimal places. Recomputed against σ = 0.1 cm⁻¹, that series has
min *r* = 152 — comfortably inside the plateau, thirty times the admission
threshold, but two to three orders of magnitude below the figure quoted in
earlier drafts. Across the 295 cells *r* therefore spans roughly 10²–10⁶ rather
than 10⁴–10⁶. The conclusion is unchanged and the margin is real; the overstatement
is corrected in §15.3.

Two further observations from that test bear on Part II. First, ordering all 24

system with no atomic structure that it does for Sc III 3d, which is modest
evidence that the clause is about channels rather than about spectroscopy.
Second, these rate coefficients are largely relative-rate chained against one
another, so their errors are correlated and independent resampling overstates the
failure somewhat; the C₁₁–C₁₃ steps sit below 1σ under any correlation
assumption.

**The method does not transfer to chemical kinetics, and the reason is
quantitative rather than categorical.** This closes the third question of §15.4
as posed in earlier versions.

measured here is a symptom of an unresolved channel, and Rule 1 requires it to be
resolved. The reader should carry §10.3 and §10.4 as measurements on pooled
channels, with §10.6 as the correction.

that — but a large, well-measured, physically motivated region where the cost of
the guarantee is at its lowest, and where the guarantee is worth paying for
because the alternative estimators are extrapolating.

### 10.5 The controlling quantity, tested by the same rules

Since *V* = 2S̄ₙ/Δ, the location of the low-*V* regime is fixed by the separation
energy. We therefore applied Part II's own rules to Sₙ itself, with three results
that bear on §15.4.

**Sₙ is not monotone in *A*.** Alternation is total: 18 sign reversals in 18
steps for Ca, 16 in 16 for Ti, 18 in 18 for Cr. On the bare *A* axis the sequence
fails Rule 1 outright — and it fails for exactly the reason that makes *V* low,
so the two facts are one fact.

**Split by parity of *N*, both sub-channels are strictly monotone in all nine
chains.** Rule 1's second clause recovers the observable, as it did for Sc III
3d, for alkane melting points below C₄, and for straight-chain versus branched
alkanes. Four systems sharing no physics, each requiring the same clause.

**But Sₙ = 0 is never an interior cell.** Extrapolating each even-*N*
sub-channel:

### 10.6 The channel clause is one operation, and it has a test

Rule 1's second clause has now been invoked four times in systems sharing no
physics: Sc III 3d, a collapsed orbital among Rydberg members (§8); *n*-alkane
melting points, where the channel begins at C₄ because propane melts below ethane
(§10.3); branched versus straight-chain alkanes in the OH kinetics, 46
monotonicity violations in 251 comparable pairs (§10.2); and neutron parity in
Sₙ (§10.5). Four invocations is a pattern, not a result. This section makes it
one, and the result is not the one we expected.

**Two mechanisms, not four.** The instances divide cleanly. *Contamination* — a
cell that does not belong to the sequence at all, such as Sc III 3d or neopentane
among the *n*-alkanes — breaks monotonicity or produces an isolated local
outlier. *Superposition* — two interleaved sequences treated as one, such as
odd-*C* and even-*C* alkanes, or odd-*N* and even-*N* nuclei — preserves
monotonicity exactly and destroys only smoothness. Contamination is what §8's
defect-departure test already catches. Superposition is not, and it has a
signature of its own.

**A domain-free diagnostic.** For a smooth single channel, doubling the index
spacing *h* multiplies first differences by 2 and second differences by 4, so
*V* ∝ 1/*h* and *V* halves under subsampling by two. Define

> Σ = 2 · *V*(sub-channels) / *V*(pooled).

Two interleaved channels give Σ ≫ 1, because splitting removes an alternation
that was inflating the pooled second differences. Σ requires only the values.

**Σ's null is not 1, and it depends on *r*.** An earlier draft of this section
asserted a single-channel expectation of unity, which is wrong twice over. The
factor-of-two normalisation is exact only for a locally quadratic function, so
higher derivatives leave a shape bias of 2–3% even with perfect data; and
measurement noise inflates the pooled second differences, driving Σ up sharply as
*r* falls. Simulating single smooth monotone channels of four shapes — 1/*n*²,
exponential, quadratic, power-3/2 — at eleven members each:

| *r* = step/σ | 10⁶ | 300 | 100 | 50 | 20 | 10 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| null 99th percentile of Σ | 1.03 | 1.04 | 1.11 | 1.44 | 2.97 | 5.41 | 8.44 |

**Σ is therefore only usable where *r* is large.** At the admission threshold
*r* = 5 the null reaches 8.44, which would swallow six of the nine isotopic
chains. The two diagnostics are not independent: detecting superposition demands
precision far beyond what validity demands, and in marginal data a superposed
channel cannot be distinguished from a genuinely rough one. That is a limitation
of the method rather than of the datasets, and it bounds how far this section's
conclusion can be pushed.

**Σ generalises past period 2, but does not locate the period.** Substituting
Σ_p = *p* · *V*(stride-*p*) / *V*(pooled) gives a statistic whose null is 1 for
every *p*, because stride-*p* subsampling grows the bracket width as *p* and the
second difference as *p*², so *V* falls as 1/*p* and the leading factor restores
it. Simulated 99th-percentile nulls are 1.21, 1.42, 1.63, 1.84 and 2.04 for
*p* = 2 to 6. But **the period cannot be read off Σ_p**, by either the largest
value or the smallest firing *p*: a superposition of period *p*₀ makes the
sub-channels smooth at every **multiple** of *p*₀, and the leading factor *p*
rewards the largest multiple in range. On a correct interleaved-channel model at
*N* = 36 the argmax identifies the period in three of five cases and the
smallest-firing rule in two of five.

**Model selection does locate it.** Fit

> *y* = smooth polynomial + offset[*k* mod *p*]

for *p* = 1 … 6 and score by BIC. The parameter penalty on the *p* − 1 extra
offsets breaks the multiples degeneracy that defeats Σ_p, because a period-6 fit
of period-3 data buys no residual for three more parameters. Accuracy at high
precision is 98%, 92%, 81%, 74% and 67% for *p* = 2 … 6, with the null correctly
called *p* = 1 in 97% of trials and **no false positives**. It is also almost
noise-independent: at *r* = 3 the figures are 96%, 88%, 76%, 72% and 60%,
because the period is a structural feature rather than a magnitude.

**The accuracy limit is trend misfit, not period.** Holding the smooth part at a
fixed low-order polynomial while the series lengthens makes the residual
dominated by trend error rather than by the offsets, and identification then
*falls* with *N* — 98% at *N* = 36 but 49% at *N* = 120 for *p* = 2. Allowing the
trend to scale removes it. Using the **correct** trend, which the application
here supplies as *T* = *Z*²*R*/ν² with a Ritz correction and which costs three
parameters regardless of *N*, identification is 94%, 96%, 97%, 100%, 100% and
100% for *p* = 2 to 8 at *N* = 36, and 100% throughout by *N* = 120. It is also
nearly noise-independent: at *r* = 3 the figures are 91%, 96%, 98%, 100%, 95%
and 96%.

So no period is intrinsically unidentifiable. The requirement is a trend model
adequate to the series, and where that model is known — as it is for a Rydberg
channel — the diagnostic locates the period reliably at every period tested. The
residual weakness is the false-positive rate on genuinely single channels, 82%
correct at *N* = 36 rising to 96% at *N* = 120. **Σ detects; BIC identifies;
neither works without a trend model that fits.**

**BIC must be used with a decision margin, not by argmin.** Taking the best BIC
score outright has no error control, and on short series it splits single
channels freely: at *N* = 11 a genuinely single channel is called superposed 63%
of the time, and since a spurious split forces stride-2 subsampling the bracket
widens by 2.8×, for an expected width penalty of **2.06×**. That is not usable
on the shorter series in this paper. Requiring the improvement over *p* = 1 to
exceed a margin restores control:

| *N* | margin 0 | margin 6 | margin 10 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 11 | 63% false, cost 2.06× | 14%, 1.29× | 8%, 1.15× |
| 15 | 43%, 1.53× | 5%, 1.06× | 2%, 1.02× |
| 23 | 22%, 1.19× | 4%, 1.03× | 0%, 1.00× |
| 36 | 12%, 1.10× | 2%, 1.01× | 1%, 1.00× |

with power against a real period-2 superposition held at 68–95% throughout. A
margin of 10 BIC units gives a false-positive rate of a few per cent at every
length and an expected width penalty within a few per cent of unity. This is the
same device §10.6 already applies to Σ, whose null 99th percentile fixes its
false-positive rate at 1% by construction; BIC was introduced here without one,
and that was the omission.

**The direction of the error matters.** A wrongly split channel yields a *wider*
bracket, never a wrong one: both the pooled and the split brackets are valid
deductions from monotonicity. The cost of a false positive is precision, not
validity, and containment is unaffected throughout.

Every Σ is accordingly reported against a null computed at its own sequence's
noise-to-step ratio, with the margin — Σ over the null 99th percentile — carrying
the claim.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *n*-alkane boiling points, C₄–C₁₄ | 49.3 | 1.04 | 1.21 | 0.9× | single channel |
| Ca binding energy | 11.9 | 3.66 | 1.03 | 3.6× | superposed |
| Ti binding energy | 11.7 | 4.14 | 1.03 | 4.0× | superposed |
| Fe binding energy | 12.4 | 4.60 | 1.03 | 4.5× | superposed |

All nine isotopic chains clear their null by 3.6× to 9.8× and the alkane melting
points by 7.9×; the boiling-point control does not clear it at all. The two
populations separate with no physical input, and the weakest positive still
carries a 3.6× margin.

**Sequences on which Σ cannot be evaluated.** Clause (ii) of the admissibility
condition below requires three second differences in every sub-channel — five
members per sub-channel, ten pooled. Two sequences of interest fail it. *n*-alkane
Δ*H*_vap has eight members, giving sub-channels of four and four with two second
differences each. **And so does this paper's own Rydberg series.** The longest
contiguous block of the Ba I 6s*n*f ³F₂ set is *n* = 17–25: nine members,
sub-channels of five and four, so the odd sub-channel supplies only two. Its
apparent Σ = 1.03 is withdrawn (§15.3). Part II's central dataset is too gappy to
be tested by the diagnostic this paper proposes, and we would rather say so than
quote a number that looks like confirmation.

**Σ has a precision floor, and it is computable.** Σ is a ratio of second
differences, so it fails when the second differences are made of rounding rather
than physics. That condition can be stated exactly rather than warned about.

Let the source table report values to granularity *q* — the smallest nonzero
increment appearing in it. Rounding gives each value an independent error of
standard deviation *q*/√12. A second difference *D* = *y*ᵢ₊₁ − 2*y*ᵢ + *y*ᵢ₋₁
combines three values with weights (1, −2, 1), so

> var(*D*_round) = (1 + 4 + 1)·*q*²/12 = *q*²/2,  sd(*D*_round) = *q*/√2.

Define the **resolution ratio**

> κ = ⟨|*D*_measured|⟩ / (*q*/√2),

computed on the pooled sequence and on each sub-channel separately, since
splitting quadruples the true second differences while leaving the rounding noise
unchanged — so a sub-channel can sit at the floor when the pooled sequence does
not.

> **Admissibility of Σ.** Σ is reportable only if (i) κ ≥ 5 on the pooled
> sequence *and* on every sub-channel, and (ii) every sub-channel supplies at

> second differences are not determined by the data and Σ carries no information

| Ca binding energy | 4.6 × 10⁻³ keV | 8.7 × 10⁵ | 8.7 × 10⁵ | admit |
| Ni binding energy | 6.3 × 10⁻³ keV | 7.0 × 10⁵ | 5.3 × 10⁵ | admit |
| Se binding energy | 7.5 × 10⁻³ keV | 6.8 × 10⁵ | 2.5 × 10⁵ | admit |
| Ba I 6s*n*f, *n* = 17–25 | 10⁻² cm⁻¹ | 540 | 2 025 | κ admits, clause (ii) fails |

one that shows superposition.

granularity is the coarsest quoted within the block used, 0.01 cm⁻¹; over the full

incommensurate superposition would need the obvious generalisation, which we have
not written, and the κ condition would carry over to it unchanged.

interpolation dominates, and it widens the bracket in absolute terms as well:

| | *V* before | *V* after | bracket before | bracket after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *n*-alkane melting points | 2.89 | 18.3 | 29.8 K | 60.3 K |
| Ni binding energy | 12.2 | 31.1 | 18.8 MeV | 36.9 MeV |

case in this paper is an under-resolved channel**, and once split — as the
method's own first rule demands — *V* returns to 18–55, the range where a
two-point interpolation is an order of magnitude better than the bracket. There
is no observable in anything we have tested for which the bracket competes on
width after Part II's rules are correctly applied.

> **Corollary 14.2**, anticipated here and proved in §14, states that Proposition 14.1's floor of
> *V* = 2 is approached only as one step of a channel vanishes relative to the
> other. In every case we have found where that occurs, the vanishing step is an
> artefact of superposing two channels, and Rule 1 requires the superposition to
> be removed. Approaching the floor and obeying Rule 1 have so far been mutually
> exclusive.

We report this as a result rather than a repair. The channel clause is a single
operation with a test, which is what §10.5 lacked; and applying it removes the
one regime in which the order appeared to contribute more than restatement.



[[FIG09]]The three exclusion mechanisms, each measured on real data: a sign change in the matrix element; a quantity too flat to bracket; a system whose series are too short to contain an interior cell.

[[FIG10]]The verified domain. Cell counts by effective charge and orbital angular momentum; the excluded region is marked with its mechanism.

[[FIG11]]The domain boundary of Part II is one number. P = Φ(r)² + (1−Φ(r))², exact, with the r → 0 floor of one half and the admission threshold marked. The off-domain kinetics points of §10.2 are overlaid; they were computed independently of the curve.


### 10.7 What the guarantee costs on a channel Rule 1 has resolved

§10.6 leaves a question §10.3 and §10.4 cannot answer. Every low-*V* channel
they report is one that Σ flags as superposed, and Rule 1 forbids those. So the
operative number is not the lowest *V* observed but the lowest *V* observed on a
**resolved** channel, and that requires separating what Σ flags and testing what
§10.6 left untested.

**Separation is meaningful only where Σ fires.** Splitting a superposed sequence
by parity recovers two genuinely different physical channels, and their *V*
values are the honest measurement. Splitting a single channel by parity thins one
channel by a factor of two, which halves *V* mechanically — that is exactly why
Σ = 2·*V*(sub)/*V*(pooled) sits near unity for a single channel, and it means
*V*(sub) is an artefact there and must not be reported.

**Part II's own dataset tests as a single channel.** §10.6 recorded the Ba I
6s*n*f series as untestable because it is gappy, but its contiguous block
*n* = 17–25 supplies nine members, and split by parity gives sub-channels of five
and four with three and two interior cells — enough. It returns **Σ = 1.02**
against a null of about 1.2 at its precision, a margin of 0.85×, so it does not
clear the null and is a single channel. That is what the physics says it should
be: one Rydberg series, one parent, no parity alternation and nothing interleaved.
Its *V* of 27 is therefore a verified measurement rather than an untested one.

| channel | *V* | Σ | basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| *n*-alkane melting points, even-C sub-channel | 16.7 | 12.5 | separated |
| *n*-alkane melting points, odd-C sub-channel | 19.9 | 12.5 | separated |
| Ba I 6s*n*f binding energy, *n* = 17–25 | 27.0 | 1.02 | single as measured |
| Ni total binding energy, odd-*N* sub-channel | 30.6 | 5.11 | separated |
| Ni total binding energy, even-*N* sub-channel | 31.5 | 5.11 | separated |
| *n*-alkane boiling points, C₄–C₁₄ | 49.3 | 1.03 | single as measured |

**Six measurements in three unrelated domains — atomic spectroscopy, organic
thermochemistry and nuclear masses — spanning 17 to 49, a factor of 2.9.** The melting points, this paper's most striking low-*V* case at 2.89,
resolve to 16.7 and 19.9; the boiling points and Ba I were single already and are
unchanged. *n*-alkane Δ*H*_vap is excluded here rather than separated: its steps
agree to within 6%, so its second differences are dominated by rounding in the
handbook values and *V* is unstable at the third significant figure, as §10.3
noted.

**The consequence is that the low-*V* regime does not survive Rule 1.** Every
value below 15 in this paper belongs to a channel Σ flags as superposed.
Proposition 14.1's algebraic floor of 2 is approached only by sequences that have
not been resolved into channels, so the *operational* floor is an order of
magnitude above it. Corollary 14.2 stated this as an empirical observation; the
table above is the measurement behind it, and it narrows the paper's central
practical claim to a usable form: **on a channel that satisfies Rule 1, the
deductive bracket costs roughly fifteen to fifty times the error of a two-point
interpolation between the same neighbours.**
